data.title: Hackers attack and penetrate Air Force’s computing platform
data.description: Hackers penetrated the Air Force’s cloud computing platform in a breach that could have exposed sensitive military information, a U.S. official said Friday. The official confirmed the hack to NBC News but could not provide any additional information about timing or the attack’s impact. “The department of the Air Force does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities, or operational status of specific networks and systems,” according to an Air Force spokesperson. Reuters first reported the cyber intrusion. “We continuously take prudent measures to protect department information, systems, and mission capabilities. Ensuring the security, resilience, and availability of our most critical war fighting assets remains a top priority,” the Air Force spokesperson added. “The department continues to assess and modernize its enterprise cloud capabilities to meet, evolving mission, security, resilience, and user requirements. Decisions regarding technical architecture, workload placement, contracts, and future capabilities are made through established governance, acquisition, and risk management processes.” This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

data.title: Cautious consumers gear up for Black Friday as inflation woes bite
data.description: NEW YORK/LOS ANGELES — Neither high fuel prices nor stubborn inflation are expected to stop U.S. shoppers from spending robustly as ​their turkey hangovers wear off on Black Friday. But below healthy top-line forecasts lie signs of stress. Holiday spending — which unofficially begins on ‌Black Friday — is seen topping last year’s strong figures by 4%-6%, several economic forecasts show. But most of the gains will be attributable to inflation which, at 3.8%, is about a percentage point higher than in each of the last two years. The National Retail Federation sees November-December holiday retail sales rising 4.2% year-over-year, to just above $1 trillion. The Mastercard Economics Institute and EY Parthenon ​each forecast sales to rise more than 5%. Eventual final results often beat pre-holiday estimates. Still, consumer sentiment remains shaky. This month, voters punished President ​Donald Trump for an Iran War that’s pushed the cost of living higher, handing Democrats sweeping electoral victories. A November survey by ⁠the National Retail Federation found that 82% of consumers are taking steps to manage holiday costs, like buying less expensive gifts. Los Angeles resident Felicia Cox, 50, said ​that while her holiday spending will be roughly stable, inflation is impacting how she thinks. “I want to get more gifts that people will actually use or need,” said ​Cox, a sales representative, while browsing in an L.A. Marshalls last week. “I feel like people aren’t able to afford as much stuff.” Worries aside, some 87% of 1,200 consumers surveyed by Deloitte in October planned to participate in the five-day shopping period from Thanksgiving through “Cyber Monday,” November 30 — the highest in a decade, according to Deloitte. “People like to spend during the holidays,” even ​when there’s a “persisting undercurrent of stress,” said Katie Thomas, who leads the Kearney Consumer Institute, part of global consulting firm Kearney. Middle- and lower-income shoppers — who have ​been trading down for months — were however more likely than wealthy ones to spend less, according to the Kearney survey. Target, Dollar Tree and Kohl’s have all pointed to belt-tightening during recent ‌earnings calls. ⁠Kohl’s CEO Michael Bender on Tuesday cited an “increasingly choiceful” consumer that is “looking to stretch every dollar.” Holiday spending forecasts mostly predated the recent stock market correction that followed the midterms, turmoil at chipmaker Nvidia, and mounting concerns around an AI bubble. The decline could dampen the wealth effect that has seen affluent shoppers splurge on gadgets and accessories, UBS analysts said in a note on Tuesday. Toys take a hit Higher input costs, particularly from petrol derivatives like plastic, are hitting some products more than others. Prices of ​toys — generally high in plastic — have risen ​13.2% since the start of the ⁠year, pushing Barbie maker Mattel this month to cut its annual forecast as consumers balked at higher costs. Some unlikely products are buoying the toy category. Best Buy and Target have both flagged trading cards — including Pokemon and Magic: The Gathering products — as a key ​growth driver. Squishy NeeDoh toys were selling for $24.99 on Amazon in October, nearly triple the price a year earlier ​on hot demand, according ⁠to e-commerce marketing platform Omnisend. Toy maker Learning Resources Inc — a plaintiff in lawsuits that overturned Trump’s tariffs — is seeing demand roughly flat, said CEO Rick Woldenberg, though he added it’s hard to predict demand before Black Friday. “People can’t shop until they have their turkey,” Woldenberg said. AI could also scramble the year’s shopping dynamics. As shoppers use AI ⁠to find bargains ​or even complete purchases — and retailers become increasingly adept at altering price quickly through AI — the deepest ​discounts could come closer to Christmas, as consumers and retailers both wait out the market, said Ryan Orabone, a consultant at Spaulding Ridge. “My advice to shoppers is to be patient,” he said. “Don’t jump on ​the first deal you see.”

data.title: Trump heads to Arizona next week to speak at a semiconductor manufacturing plant
data.description: WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump, who has staked his economic policy on growth in the artificial intelligence sector, will travel to Arizona on Dec. 4 to speak at the groundbreaking for a new Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. computer chip foundry, according to both the White House and the Taiwan-based company. The trip will come at the end of a week where AI comes under the microscope in Washington in the aftermath of Trump intervening to get his ally Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia. Huang is slated to testify at a Senate Banking Committee hearing on Dec. 3 and will face questions about how his company has been selling its chips abroad — and his affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Beijing has denied it. TSMC has expanded aggressively in the Phoenix, Arizona, area, using its U.S. facilities to manufacture chips for tech companies such as Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Broadcom, and Qualcomm. Trump is attending the start of construction on the fifth phase of TSMC’s expansion in Arizona. TSMC in July announced plans to spend another $100 billion on expanding its manufacturing capacity in the United States, bringing its total pledged investment in American chipmaking to $265 billion. The size of the investment has grown as the development of artificial intelligence has stimulated demand for more computer chips, at the same time as Taiwan’s dominance in chipmaking has led countries including the U.S. to address supply chain vulnerabilities by producing more domestically. While Trump has sought to promote the investments as a function of his tariffs, the company began construction in Arizona during the presidency of Democrat Joe Biden. The bipartisan CHIPS and Science Act, signed into law by Biden, also helped to provide some financial support for the project. The White House said the expansion would enable the creation of 10,000 direct jobs and another 11,000 indirect jobs in the wider community. The site currently accounts for more than 12,000 construction jobs.

data.title: Why more American tech startups are ditching Silicon Valley for China’s Shenzhen
data.description: SHENZHEN, China — In the intense world of technology startups, where even the smallest cost and time-saving measures draw the line between success and failure, several American companies are leaving Silicon Valley behind and opting for the Chinese megacity of Shenzhen. Many of these entrepreneurs cite the proximity of part suppliers, engineers and manufacturers, which allows them to design and refine products at speeds that they say are not possible back home. Developing technology in China saves valuable time and costs, they say, because in the U.S. manufacturing expertise can be hard to find and companies have to wait for the parts to be shipped out of China anyway. “When you want to develop hardware, you don’t have to really go outside,” said Nicolo Micheletti, a founding engineer at the San Francisco-based smart wearables company Mentra. He said companies known as original design manufacturers, or ODMs, which design and manufacture products that other companies sell as their own, operate in Shenzhen, along with other suppliers. As a result, he said, virtually everything required to build a product is a taxi ride away from his office. Shenzhen was thrust into the spotlight last week when it hosted the APEC summit and a historic trilateral meeting attended by President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin. Known as a hub for cutting-edge innovation, in Shenzhen driverless taxis ferry passengers around and delivery drones carry takeout bubble tea. But the futuristic metropolis of 18 million people, just north of Hong Kong, was a fishing village half a century ago. It underwent a rapid transformation after it became the first Chinese city allowed to engage in free enterprise under the country’s economic reform in the late ‘70s. Riding on the manufacturing might of China’s southeastern Guangdong province, where it is situated, and with the government’s support, Shenzhen became one of the world’s wealthiest cities as it churned out cheap electronics, toys and clothes for big foreign brands. In 2020, Xi described the city as “a miracle in the world development history.” But the focus increasingly turned toward homegrown innovation, in part due to its comprehensive supply chain, lower costs, transport links and proximity to Hong Kong, long known as a regional financial powerhouse. Today, Shenzhen boasts almost as many billionaires as New York, is home to tech giants such as Huawei, Tencent and BYD, and is seeing a growing number of entrepreneurs choosing to leave California’s Silicon Valley and set up there. The city can be daunting for newcomers, especially as dealing with suppliers and manufacturers, navigating the labyrinth of electronics markets and filtering potential partners often requires a knowledge of Mandarin. Much of the venture capital is also still concentrated in Silicon Valley. Heather Nelson, an MIT graduate who works at Domayn, an early-stage neurotechnology company, said the sheer speed at which their team is able to develop their product makes it all worthwhile. “It’s enabling us to create something that I think is really special, something that we really care about, something that helps people’s brain health,” she said, adding: “We can do that so quickly and also more cheaply.” The mechanical engineer and New Jersey native added that it was not impossible to build a company in the U.S., but said, “You just can’t do that in America anymore at the same speed and at the same cost.” Hiteyjit Gujral, the co-founder of the San Francisco-based startup Voyage, agreed that “in a space like this, time is money.” “You don’t want to spend time on waiting for components, waiting a week to get something only to realize that it’s wrong and then wait another week,” said Gujral, whose company is attempting to build “wearables for the mind” that would allow users to control devices just by thinking. He said that when everything is coming from Shenzhen, the technology is so new that his team has to iterate on the hardware rapidly. Henk Werner, who runs a membership-based startup incubator called Troublemaker, said the spirit of cooperation is also a big plus. He said that if his designers finish a drawing at 1 a.m., they can send it to a factory and have a prototype by 7 a.m. “Everyone is so open to cooperate, to make money together. Because people here need you to make a product and sell it,” he added. “And you need them for their expertise in manufacturing and doing products in a good quality, fast.” Despite the enthusiasm shown by developers, tensions have been simmering between China and the U.S., which seemingly have reached a truce in their escalating trade conflict. A September report from the Department of State warned that China “remained one of the world’s most closed major economies” and revisions made to the country’s Foreign Trade Law in March expanded “export controls, sanctions, and other measures to goods, technology, and services, including education, tourism, and other major U.S. exports to China.” The report said that American companies had “reported increased anxiety about operating in China” for a number of reasons, including “a restrictive business environment” and the government’s “expansion and increasingly aggressive use of legal and regulatory authorities to target foreign companies and individuals.” China remained on the Office of the United States Trade Representative’s priority watchlist “for serious deficiencies in its intellectual property regime,” the report added, referring to regular American complaints that China engages in widespread intellectual property theft, forced technology transfer and cyberespionage. The recent scandal surrounding the resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO also put a spotlight on the U.S.-China relations. U.S. intelligence agencies determined that Huang, a close ally of President Donald Trump, was in an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy. The pair are not related. Huang has been one of the loudest proponents of free-flowing sales of chips to China and his return sets up a potential conflict with regulators both inside and outside the Trump administration who wish to impede sales of the advanced AI hardware to the country. Back in Shenzhen, it is not just developers and suppliers that are increasingly setting roots in the city. Investors are moving in too. “This is completely the land of opportunity for this century,” said Taylor Ogan, chief executive of Snow Bull Capital, a hedge fund that invests in Chinese technology companies. For Ogan, being in Shenzhen means he can inspect in person almost every part of the supply chain of companies he’s investing in, something he said would be much harder to do if he were back in the U.S., as most of the hardware supply chain is in China. “There are still a lot of great ideas from Silicon Valley companies,” said Ogan, who is originally from Colorado. “Don’t get me wrong. But they’re all manufactured here.” Tom Llamas, Janis Mackey Frayer, Dawn Liu, Erin Tan and Ignacio Torres reported from Shenzhen, China. Mithil Aggarwal reported from Hong Kong.

data.title: Judge blocks FCC review of ABC station licenses for now
data.description: The Walt Disney Co. secured a temporary restraining order Wednesday blocking the Federal Communications Commission from moving forward with an unusually early review of ABC’s broadcast-station licenses, which the media company has called an attack on free speech by the Trump administration. U.S. District Judge Loren L. AliKhan’s decision is the latest turn in the legal battle between Disney and the FCC, the federal agency that regulates the broadcast airwaves. Disney filed a lawsuit against the FCC in August, calling the early license review an “existential threat” to the First Amendment. The FCC “wants to stop, censor [and] control” what ABC can broadcast, Disney lawyer Beth Wilkinson told AliKhan at a hearing on Oct. 6. Wilkinson characterized FCC Chairman Brendan Carr’s actions as a series of “unending threats.” The FCC’s lawyers argued at the hearing that the U.S. District Court does not have jurisdiction in the matter, accusing ABC of trying to circumvent the federal regulatory process. In her order temporarily blocking the agency’s moves on Wednesday, the judge wrote that she concluded that Disney was “likely to succeed on their retaliation claim” against the FCC, as well as casting the “early license renewal proceedings as a retaliatory act.” The courtroom confrontation stems from the FCC’s April 28 order directing Disney’s eight owned-and-operated TV stations to file their broadcast license renewals ahead of schedule. The licenses were not due to come up for renewal until 2028 at the earliest. Carr has said that order was tied to the agency’s investigation into Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion practices. It came a day after President Donald Trump called on ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel over a joke he had made about first lady Melania Trump. The FCC is also reviewing whether ABC’s “The View” broke a requirement that broadcast stations give equal time to political candidates for the same office. Disney has argued that the talk show qualifies as a “bona fide news” program, meaning it is exempt from the equal-time rule. In a phone interview with NBC News after Disney filed suit, Carr said he believed Disney’s challenge to the FCC’s order was a “meritless case.” In remarks at the agency’s open commission meeting last week, Carr said the suit was filed “in the wrong court” at “the wrong time.” ABC Owned Television Stations, a division of Disney Entertainment Television, operates stations in New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Philadelphia, Houston, San Francisco, the Raleigh-Durham area, and Fresno, California. The Oct. 6 hearing featured one notably light-hearted exchange. “We don’t want to be here,” said Wilkinson, the Disney lawyer. “I don’t want to be here either,” said AlkiKhan, the judge. The Walt Disney Company and the FCC did not immediately return requests for comment on Wednesday’s ruling.

data.title: SpaceX gets green light to deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space
data.description: The Federal Communications Commission is authorizing Elon Musk’s SpaceX to deploy a constellation of 1 million satellites for data centers in space, the agency said on Wednesday. SpaceX earlier this year sought permission to deploy up to 1 million orbital compute modules to process massive amounts of data to be used on Earth. The FCC said it was approving the SpaceX “Starmind” constellation to help meet rapidly growing demand for AI computing. Under the license, SpaceX must begin deployment no later than November 2033, deploy 10% of the maximum number — or 100,000 — no later than November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038, the FCC said. Approving the application will permit SpaceX “to pioneer emergent technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence,” the FCC added. Data centers are the physical backbone of artificial intelligence, requiring massive amounts of power. “By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers,” SpaceX told the FCC. It was unclear whether SpaceX would put 1 million satellites in space, where only 17,000 satellites exist currently. Satellite operators sometimes request approval for higher numbers of satellites than they intend to deploy to buy design flexibility. SpaceX sought approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites before it began deployment of that system. The growing network currently has just over 11,000 satellites in space. SpaceX’s request bets heavily on reduced costs of Starship, the company’s next-generation reusable rocket under development, to help deploy satellites. Amazon’s rival satellite unit Leo and others have criticized the plan, suggesting SpaceX was unlikely to deploy all the satellites and that it could take centuries to do so. FCC Chair Brendan Carr rejected that criticism in March. “Amazon should focus on getting Amazon’s house in order with their own launches and their own satellite constellation, rather than worrying about other people that are actually out there ​launching satellites at the pace and cadence that SpaceX is,” Carr said. The FCC said it was also approving SpaceX’s requests to back up its optical network by approving additional communications.

data.title: Market sell-off picks up steam, as Jensen Huang’s Nvidia return fails to calm AI fears
data.description: U.S. stocks fell sharply Wednesday, led by companies linked to the artificial intelligence boom. The moves largely erased the historic rally Monday that was sparked by Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s CEO. As of early Wednesday, the Nasdaq 100 index was down more than 4%, the S&P 500 gave up nearly 3%, and the Dow fell 900 points. Shares of Nvidia slid 7%. The action marked a stark reversal from Monday, when financial markets staged their biggest one-day rally since April 2025. The Nasdaq 100 skyrocketed 6.8% and the S&P 500 surged 4.7%. Monday’s rally was primarily driven by Nvidia, one of the world’s largest AI chip design firms, which announced the surprise return of CEO Jensen Huang despite an ongoing scandal involving multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. The return of Huang, a de facto ambassador for the AI industry, briefly reassured investors that big AI firms, and the trillions of dollars they borrow and lend, would continue to grow without interruption. But the good vibes didn’t last. “The risk-off tone has returned over the last 24 hours, as Monday’s rebound in tech stocks lost momentum once again,” said Deutsche Bank strategists in a note early Wednesday. “Clearly the latest declines have revived questions as to whether this selloff has further to run,” they said. Before Monday’s rally, stocks had faced weeks of selling which pushed the Nasdaq 100 into correction territory. The index fell further on Wednesday, into bear market territory, which is when an index falls 20% or more from its most recent high. Shares of semiconductor and computer memory companies were the biggest drags on Wednesday, along with Nvidia, down between 7% and 10% in early trading. AI-related sentiment was damaged further by frontier AI developer Anthropic, whose shares have spiraled lower since its IPO last week. After a strong market debut Friday, with shares closing higher by more than 17%, Anthropic shares have been marred by three straight days of losses. Anthropic’s shares are now about 10% below its IPO price, and almost 25% below where it closed on its first day, tumbling to $78 per share. Stocks Wednesday likely faced additional pressure due to the looming Thanksgiving holiday. U.S. markets will be closed Thursday and open for only a half-day of trading Friday. Investors are more likely to cut their large or risky trades before extended weekends, in order to avoid being trapped in positions while events unfold. New tariffs fuel uncertainty On top of cracks in the AI sector, “matters weren’t helped by the latest tariff headlines,” Deutsche Bank’s team wrote. On Wednesday, the Trump administration unveiled a new wave of tariffs on the United States’ top trading partners, such as the European Union, China, Japan, and a dozen more. “It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind,” wrote ING senior trade economist Inga Fechner in a note on Wednesday. That drove stocks down further, with the prospect that more tariffs could cause renewed trade tensions, a renewed inflation spike and cause a flare up with a policy that had largely started to subside in recent months. Even before Wednesday’s formal announcement, a spokesperson for China’s commerce ministry blasted the new import duties. “Tariff wars and trade wars are in the interests of neither side,” a ministry spokesperson said. The ministry called it “political manipulation.” “Some investors might have been caught off guard by news that the Administration is on track to release more tariffs, but the key question about the Administration unveiling new tariffs from the Section 301 overcapacity investigation has never been an issue of whether but when,” wrote Sarah Bianchi, chief strategist of international political affairs, at Evercore ISI. Inflation is still climbing Compounding the negative pressure facing investors on Wednesday, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge moved further away from the Fed’s 2% goal. The Personal Consumption Expenditures index was 3.8% for October, up from 3.6% in September. Even excluding food and energy, the “core” inflation reading rose to 3.3%. It had been 3.1% the previous month. A rise in core inflation readings is particularly noteworthy for economists because it can indicate that high prices from energy costs are spilling over into the rest of the economy. It also raises the likelihood that the Fed will raise interest rates at its next meeting, which concludes with a rate decision on Dec. 9. Last week, a top Fed policymaker said the central bank needed to “shock people” with a larger rate hike than is typical. “I’m very, very concerned about inflation,” Fed governor Christoper Waller said in a CNBC interview. “It’s kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out.” Waller said the Fed needed to take “more aggressive actions,” such as hiking by 0.50%, more than the Fed’s usual 0.25% rate increase. “You might need to, like, shock people,” Waller said. A rate hike would carry its own complications, however. As trillion-dollar tech giants borrow hundreds of billions of dollars to build out AI data centers and chips, any increase to interest rates could quickly raise their massive costs. It could also hurt an already pained U.S. consumer. Mortgage rates continue to hover well above 7%, and a rate hike could push borrowing costs higher for auto loans, credit cards, personal loans, and other forms of credit.

data.title: Trump proposes a new wave of tariffs on China, E.U. and other trade partners
data.description: The Trump administration on Tuesday proposed a new wave of tariffs on the European Union, China and other trade partners, the result of a probe into what it says are unfair manufacturing subsidies. Some of the proposals include tariffs of at least 20% on China, which would match an agreement reached with the White House. But the duties could reach up to 40% if talks between the countries fail. The tariffs will be implemented under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a statute that the White House has relied upon more frequently for trade authority ever since the Supreme Court blocked many of Trump’s 2025 country-specific tariffs, imposed under a different authority. In announcing the details of the new duties, the U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the overall rates applied to each trading partner would not surpass levels that were previously agreed to as part of bilateral framework trade deals. “When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points,” Greer said on CNBC. “So what we’re proposing today are actually a set of targeted tariffs to respond to this problem of excess capacity,” he added. For example, Trump agreed to cap tariffs on European Union imports at 15% as part of a deal reached in 2025. On Wednesday, the USTR reiterated that cap. The new tariffs will not stack on top of existing duties, except for the case of China. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this,” Greer said. “They know what we’re proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don’t think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple of months from now.” Greer said he expects that “a broad” negotiation with trading partners would follow today’s proposals. But tensions continue to flare with trading partners, especially between Canada, the EU and China. Just weeks ago, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer accused the EU of “aggressively” supporting Airbus and said that a loan from the European Investment Bank to the French aerospace giant threatened to inject “substantial uncertainty into transatlantic trade in the aerospace sector.” The EU rejected Greer’s assertion, saying the loan was normal and he had “really no grounds” to question it. The bloc, made up of 27 countries, is the United States’ largest trading partner. Meanwhile, in August, trade talks with Canada collapsed after Prime Minister Mark Carney said the Trump administration requested “uneconomic” and unfair terms at the last minute. Carney recalled his negotiators to Ottawa and for more than three months the two sides have traded verbal barbs. Canada is the country’s third largest trading partner, according to data through September of this year. Recently, informal talks resumed between the U.S. and Canada but a formal deal does not yet appear to be within reach. On Wednesday, Greer said those talks with Canada were continuing, due to some outstanding “sticking points.” Another key U.S. trading partner, Mexico, was not included in Wednesday’s tariff proposals. “I think the most important one where we’re still going through the investigation process, is Mexico,” Greer told CNBC. “I think it’ll be a little bit more time before we release that report,” he said.

data.title: Chinese tech giant Huawei convicted of federal charges, including fraud
data.description: Chinese tech giant Huawei was convicted of multiple federal charges in New York on Tuesday after prosecutors accused the company of stealing technology from U.S. companies, abusing the American financial system and helping Iran spy on its citizens. A jury in New York’s Eastern District found the company and three of its subsidiaries guilty of seven conspiracy counts that included bank fraud, wire fraud, money laundering, defrauding the United States and conspiracy to steal trade secrets. In the roughly two-month trial, Huawei was also convicted of bank fraud and wire fraud. Huawei was acquitted of two counts, a racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice. “For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft and deception,” Assistant Attorney General Tysen A. Duva said in a statement. “Huawei’s crimes threatened the U.S. financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market, and undermined our national security.” In a statement, Huawei said the charges are “without legal or factual merit,” and it said it welcomes the racketeering verdict. “We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests,” the company said. Huawei attorney Brian Heberling said the company plans to appeal. At sentencing, which is scheduled for Sept. 14, Huawei could face fines, forfeiture and restitution. Prosecutors accused the company, which makes smartphones and has telecom networks around the world, of encouraging its workforce of 200,000 in 170 countries to lie, cheat, and steal “for a competitive advantage to grow and protect its business.” Huawei was accused of misappropriating intellectual property like source code, user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology and robot testing technology, prosecutors said. T-Mobile, Cisco, Quintel and CNEX were among the companies whose technology was stolen, federal prosecutors said in a news release Tuesday. In Iran, the company assisted the regime with “turnkey” internet services and mobile networks, prosecutors said, and it provided surveillance cameras that allowed officials to monitor protests. Huawei also helped intelligence agents monitor and censor the internet, prosecutors said. Huawei then lied to banks about the nature of its business in Iran, allowing the company to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and become what prosecutors described as “a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services.” In an interview Tuesday, Heberling rejected the government’s allegations, saying prosecutors presented a “caricature-like portrait” of Huawei of as a corrupt organization with company policies that condoned crime. “That was just profoundly inconsistent with the company that I experienced in my work, but more importantly, [with] the evidence, which really showed a series of isolated events over a 20-year period,” he said. “No company can insure perfection over that period of time.” Heberling argued that the racketeering acquittal — the most serious charge the company faced — showed a “profound rejection of the narrative the United States pursued in this case.” Huawei was previously banned from selling equipment to U.S. carriers over fears that it poses a security risk, according to the Associated Press, and it was blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and Britain. China’s foreign ministry said Wednesday that Beijing opposed U.S. efforts to suppress Chinese companies. “The Chinese government firmly opposes the U.S. suppression and containment of Chinese companies and firmly supports Chinese companies in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a regular press briefing, when asked about the verdict.

data.title: Jensen Huang says he’s thankful for second chance at Nvidia employee meeting
data.description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made a triumphant return to the semiconductor giant in an all-hands meeting Tuesday morning, apologizing to staff for his conduct during his previous stint at the company’s helm and vowing to do better this time around. No company has impacted the world as deeply or profoundly as Nvidia, Huang said, according to an Nvidia employee who attended the meeting. Huang called the company’s story the most interesting in the world. According to the individual, Huang expressed contrition for his past behavior and was adamant that employees should follow the company’s code of conduct. The AI hardware leader resigned from the company on Nov. 12 amid mounting scrutiny about alleged romantic relationships with subordinates and Alice Huang, a former executive at Singaporean cloud computing company Megaspeed. According to U.S. intelligence officials, Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. He also said that he has been regularly attending therapy and that he had been deeply embarrassed about recent events, the source said. The CEO was met with an overwhelmingly positive reception, even receiving a standing ovation, according to the source. Huang’s return marked a nearly unprecedented case of corporate whiplash. After a wave of reports emerged stating that Huang had been involved in extramarital relationships — potentially with someone accused of being a Chinese intelligence asset — Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife in a letter sent to Nvidia employees and shared online on Nov. 8. “To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” Huang wrote at the time. “I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.” Huang issued a personal statement on Nov. 17, expressing remorse but professing his admiration for and dedication to Nvidia. Huang founded the semiconductor designer in 1993 and grew it into what was once the world’s most valuable company. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang wrote in that statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Less than a week later, Nvidia’s board announced that Huang would return to the company — backed by “input from senior levels of the United States government” that essentially guaranteed “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Huang said in Tuesday’s meeting that President Donald Trump supported the company. “President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang said, according to the Nvidia employee. Huang said that Nvidia was an apolitical company. Huang added that he returned as CEO because the board — and not the government — had wanted him to be reinstalled. The meeting, which kicked off around 9:30 a.m., lasted around an hour, according to the source, who added that Huang exited to the Foo Fighters’ song “Times Like These.”
